body.statement:
For every \(j\in\mathbb N\), the interval \(C_{\alpha,j}(Z)\) has exact finite-sample uniform coverage
\[
 \inf_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}
 \Pr_x\{\ell(x)\in C_{\alpha,j}(Z)\}\ge 1-\alpha.
\]
Its deterministic half-length satisfies
\[
 s_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}
 \operatorname{cv}_{\alpha}\!\left(
   b_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}/s_{r_{\mathrm{CI},j}}
 \right)
 \le (1+j^{-1})
 \inf_{r\in\mathcal R_+}
 s_r\operatorname{cv}_{\alpha}(b_r/s_r).
\]
Writing \(r_\alpha=\sqrt{\log\{1+(1-2\alpha)^2\}}\) and
\(c_\alpha=(1-2\alpha)r_\alpha/2\), uniformly over the stated design range,
\[
 c_\alpha\omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1)
 \le \operatorname{EL}^{\star}_{\alpha}
 \le \liminf_{j\to\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}}
 \mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C_{\alpha,j}(Z)]
 \le
 \{1+2\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\}
 \omega_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{nest}}}(1).
\]
body.justification: The theorem delivers exact coverage and explicit global expected-length constants for a total bias-aware interval under the causal score experiment.
body.gap: The nested score operator is instantiated here, while its conversion to a closed-form calendar rate is deliberately left open.
body.consumer: Use the interval generated by the covariance-weighted modulus; its reported length is benchmarked against every uniformly honest interval.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(j\), abbreviate \(r=r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\), \(b=b_r\), and \(s=s_r>0\),
and let
\(a_x=\mathbb E_x[\widehat\theta_r]-\ell(x)\).  By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}score\text{-}covariance}\), the estimator is Gaussian.
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}total\text{-}modulus\text{-}rule}\), its standard
deviation is exactly \(s\) and \(|a_x|\le b\) for every
\(x\in\mathcal M_{T,m}\).  Hence
\[
 \frac{\widehat\theta_r-\ell(x)}s
 \sim\mathcal N(t_x,1),
 \qquad t_x=a_x/s,
 \qquad |t_x|\le b/s.
\]
For \(c\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), set
\(g_c(t)=\Pr\{|\mathcal N(t,1)|\le c\}
=\Phi(c-t)+\Phi(c+t)-1\).  Its derivative is
\(g_c'(t)=\phi(c+t)-\phi(c-t)\le0\), because
\((c+t)^2\ge(c-t)^2\).  Symmetry gives \(g_c(t)=g_c(-t)\).
The definition of \(\operatorname{cv}_\alpha\) therefore implies
\[
 \Pr_x\!\left{
   |\widehat\theta_r-\ell(x)|
   \le s\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b/s)
 \right}
 \ge1-\alpha.
\]
This is the asserted finite-sample uniform coverage.  The half-length is
deterministic and equals
\(s_r\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b_r/s_r)\); its factor
\(1+j^{-1}\) inequality is exactly the defining inequality for
\(r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\) in
\(\mathrm{def{:}affine\text{-}estimator}\).

Let \(z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha/2)\).  For every \(t\ge0\), the interval
\([-t-z_\alpha,t+z_\alpha]\) contains
\([t-z_\alpha,t+z_\alpha]\), so
\(\Pr\{|\mathcal N(t,1)|\le t+z_\alpha\}\ge1-\alpha\).  Thus
\(\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(t)\le t+z_\alpha\).  We next verify directly
that radius one is admissible.  With \(e=(\mathbf 1_T,0)\), adding \(ae\)
preserves membership in \(2\mathcal M_{T,m}\), because it changes none of
the Holder differences or deviation coordinates.  The set \(O\) is
nonempty by \(\mathrm{ass{:}index\text{-}range}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}terminal\text{-}range}\).  Since \(\ell(e)=1\) and
\(Ke=\mathbf 1_O\ne0\), a radius-one maximizer with slack Mahalanobis norm
could be improved by adding a sufficiently small positive multiple of
\(e\).  Hence its norm constraint is active.  The same direction shows that
\(w\) is unbounded; concavity and monotonicity then imply \(w'_+(1)>0\),
since a zero right derivative would make \(w\) constant thereafter.  Thus
\(1\in\mathcal R_+\).  The supergradient inequality at one gives
\(w(0)\le w(1)-s_1\), where \(s_1=w'_+(1)\).  Therefore
\(0<s_1\le w(1)\) and \(b_1=\{w(1)-s_1\}/2\ge0\).  Consequently
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 2s_1\operatorname{cv}_\alpha(b_1/s_1)
 &\le 2b_1+2z_\alpha s_1\\
 &=w(1)+(2z_\alpha-1)s_1\\
 &\le \{1+2z_\alpha\}w(1).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Using the infimum-approaching property of \(r_{\mathrm{CI},j}\) and the
fact that the interval length is nonrandom gives
\[
 \liminf_{j\to\infty}\sup_x
 \mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C_{\alpha,j}(Z)]
 \le \{1+2z_\alpha\}w(1).
\]
Every \(C_{\alpha,j}\) is admissible in the definition of
\(\operatorname{EL}^\star_\alpha\), so that definition also gives the
middle inequality.

It remains to prove the lower bound for every uniformly honest interval,
not merely for affine intervals.  Set
\[
 r_\alpha=\sqrt{\log\{1+(1-2\alpha)^2\}}.
\]
Because \(0<1-2\alpha<1\), one has \(0<r_\alpha<\sqrt{\log2}<1\).
Take the canonical endpoints \(x^-_{r_\alpha},x^+_{r_\alpha}\), whose
target separation is \(\Delta_\alpha=w(r_\alpha)\).  The same direct
Gaussian likelihood-ratio calculation as above yields
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)
 \le\frac12\sqrt{e^{r_\alpha^2}-1}
 =\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
If \(C\) is any interval with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) at both
endpoints, then, under \(P_-\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr_-\{\ell(x^-_{r_\alpha}),\ell(x^+_{r_\alpha})\in C\}
 &\ge 1-2\alpha-\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)\\
 &\ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
On this event the interval has length at least \(\Delta_\alpha\).  Hence
\[
 \sup_x\mathbb E_x[\operatorname{length}C]
 \ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}w(r_\alpha).
\]
Finally, concavity and nonnegativity give
\[
 w(r_\alpha)
 \ge r_\alpha w(1)+(1-r_\alpha)w(0)
 \ge r_\alpha w(1).
\]
Taking the infimum over all uniformly honest intervals proves
\(\operatorname{EL}^\star_\alpha\ge c_\alpha w(1)\), where
\(c_\alpha=(1-2\alpha)r_\alpha/2\).  The constants depend only on
\(\alpha\), so the conclusion is uniform over the full stated design range.
